question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Sumptuous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Inexpensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Sumptuous" means extremely expensive, luxurious and lavish, especially in relation to food, clothes or surroundings. (अत्यंत खर्चीला/भव्य)
◦ Example: The hotel served a sumptuous banquet to its guests.

• Its antonym must convey the opposite idea, i.e. cheap, plain or costing little. "Inexpensive" means not costing a great deal of money, which is the direct opposite of "sumptuous". (सस्ता)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Unremitting" means never relaxing or slackening; constant and persistent — this describes duration or effort, and has no connection with cost or luxury.

• Option 2: "Lucrative" means producing a great deal of profit. This is close in spirit to "sumptuous" (both suggest richness), so it is a near-associate, not an opposite.

• Option 4: "Delectable" means delicious or highly pleasing, especially of food — this is actually a near-synonym of "sumptuous" when the word describes a feast, not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Sumptuous": lavish, luxurious, opulent, splendid, palatial, extravagant.

• Other common antonym pairs frequently tested by SSC: Frugal x Extravagant, Austere x Luxurious, Meagre x Abundant, Modest x Ostentatious.

question:
Select the meaningful and correctly spelt word from the given options to fill in the blank.
The chief guest is ____________ to arrive at the venue within half an hour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. expected.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct word for the blank is "expected", meaning regarded as likely to happen or arrive. The sentence means the chief guest is likely/anticipated to arrive within half an hour, which fits the context perfectly.

• The correct spelling is EX + PECT + ED, derived from the Latin exspectare, meaning "to look out for, await". Only this option is both meaningful in context and correctly spelt.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "accepted" is correctly spelt but is not meaningful in this context — "accepted" means agreed to receive or approve of something, which does not fit a guest's arrival.

• Option 2: "expieted" is not a correctly spelt English word at all — it is a meaningless jumble of letters resembling "expected".

• Option 4: "espected" is also a misspelling; the "x" of "expected" has been wrongly dropped and replaced.

NOTE

• SSC frequently tests such "meaningful and correctly spelt word" questions where two or three options are plausible-looking misspellings of the intended word — always check the meaning first, then the spelling.

• Commonly confused/misspelt exam words: separate (not seperate), definitely (not definately), occurred (not occured), embarrass (not embarass), accommodate (not accomodate).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Peter was brought in the penalty area.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. was brought down in the.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In football/sporting usage, the phrasal expression "to be brought down" means to be knocked or pulled to the ground by an opponent, typically through a foul or tackle.

• The original sentence "Peter was brought in the penalty area" is incomplete and ungrammatical — the verb "brought" needs the particle "down" to make sense, giving: "Peter was brought down in the penalty area", meaning Peter was fouled/tackled to the ground inside the penalty area (the standard commentary phrase used when a penalty is awarded).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "was brought down of the" is incorrect because the preposition "of" does not collocate with "penalty area"; the correct preposition of place here is "in".

• Option 2: "was brought of the" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 1 (wrong preposition "of"), and it also drops the essential particle "down".

• Option 3: "was brought on the" wrongly uses the preposition "on" instead of "in", and also omits "down", which is essential to the meaning of a foul.

NOTE

• Other sports-commentary phrasal verbs commonly tested: "sent off" (dismissed from the game), "brought on" (substituted into the game), "called off" (a match cancelled), "knocked out" (eliminated from a tournament).

• Always check whether a phrasal verb's particle (down/up/off/on) has been dropped — SSC frequently sets a distractor that changes only the preposition while removing the necessary particle.

question:
Identify the error in the use of preposition in the given sentence and select the correct option.
Radhika is not capable on participating in a national level competition.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: The adjective "capable" always takes the preposition "of" before a gerund/noun, i.e. "capable of + V-ing/noun", meaning having the ability or power to do something.

• Applying the rule: "Radhika is not capable on participating" must be corrected to "Radhika is not capable of participating in a national level competition."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "about" is incorrect — "capable about" is not an accepted collocation in English.

• Option 3: "on" is incorrect — this is the very error present in the original sentence; "on" does not follow "capable".

• Option 4: "at" is incorrect — "capable at" is not a standard English collocation; "at" typically follows words like "good/bad/skilled" (e.g. "good at"), not "capable".

NOTE

• Other adjectives that take a fixed preposition tested frequently by SSC: fond of, afraid of, proud of, tired of, aware of, confident of/about, keen on, dependent on, good at, skilled in, interested in, angry with (a person)/at (a thing).

• "Capable" should not be confused with "able", which is followed directly by a to-infinitive ("able to participate"), not "of".

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
They cancelled the meeting due to bad weather.
option_1: The meeting is cancelled by them because of bad weather.
option_2: The meeting was cancelled due to bad weather.
option_3: They cancelled the meeting and bad weather was the cause.
option_4: The bad weather is the reason they cancelled the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The meeting was cancelled due to bad weather.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "They cancelled the meeting due to bad weather" is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 (+ by + Subject, if needed)

• Applying the rule: the object "the meeting" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary used is "was"; the verb "cancelled" (already V2/V3 for this regular verb) is retained; the reason phrase "due to bad weather" is carried over unchanged, and the impersonal agent "they" can be safely dropped as it adds no information.
◦ Passive: The meeting was cancelled due to bad weather.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 wrongly uses "is cancelled", which is Simple Present Tense passive, not Simple Past — the tense of the original sentence has been changed.

• Option 3 is simply the active sentence restructured with "and"; it is not a passive construction at all, since there is no "be + V3" form.

• Option 4 again uses "is the reason", a present tense active construction, and does not convert the main verb "cancelled" into the passive at all.

NOTE

• When the doer of the action is unimportant, unknown, or obvious (as with "they" used impersonally), the "by + agent" phrase is usually dropped in the passive voice.

• Do not confuse voice (active/passive) with tense — converting voice must always preserve the original tense of the sentence.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The work will be finished by the mason within a short time.
option_1: The mason will be finishing the work within a short time.
option_2: The mason would have finish the work within a short time.
option_3: The mason would finish the work within a short time.
option_4: The mason will finish the work within a short time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The mason will finish the work within a short time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The work will be finished by the mason" is in the Simple Future Tense (passive).

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "the mason" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "will" is retained as in the original; the past participle "finished" is changed to its base form "finish"; and the passive subject "the work" becomes the object.
◦ Active: The mason will finish the work within a short time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 wrongly uses the continuous form "will be finishing", which changes the tense from Simple Future to Future Continuous — not permitted when merely converting voice.

• Option 2 is grammatically broken — "would have finish" mixes the modal "would have" (used for Past Perfect-type conditionals) with the bare form "finish" instead of a past participle, and also wrongly changes "will" to "would".

• Option 3 incorrectly changes the modal auxiliary from "will" to "would", altering the tense/mood of the original sentence from simple future to a conditional sense.

NOTE

• When converting passive to active, the auxiliary verb of the original sentence (will/can/may/must, etc.) must be retained exactly, only the "be + V3" pattern is replaced by the base form (V1) of the verb.

• Common trap: distractor options change the modal verb (will → would/should) or the aspect (simple → continuous/perfect) instead of only changing the voice.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Memory like a sieve
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Poor memory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a memory like a sieve" means a very poor or forgetful memory, i.e. a tendency to forget things easily. (बहुत कमज़ोर याददाश्त होना)
◦ Example: I have a memory like a sieve these days — I keep forgetting where I put my keys.

• The image behind the idiom is that of a sieve, which is full of holes and cannot hold anything poured into it — just as a sieve lets things fall through, a person with such a memory cannot "hold on to" information.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Being healthy" has no connection with memory or forgetfulness; it is unrelated to the idiom.

• Option 3: "Feeling ill" is also unrelated — the idiom concerns mental recall, not physical health.

• Option 4: "Remembering everything" is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning — it describes an excellent memory, whereas "a memory like a sieve" describes a poor one.

NOTE

• Other memory-related idioms tested by SSC: "To slip one's mind" (to be forgotten), "To ring a bell" (to sound familiar), "To have a memory like an elephant" (an excellent memory — the opposite of "like a sieve").

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the following sentence.
He will be looking as if he has not slept.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. He looks.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule: Verbs of appearance/perception such as look, seem, feel, sound, when followed by the conjunction "as if / as though" to describe a person's present appearance or state, are conventionally used in the Simple Present Tense, even though the situation being described may feel hypothetical.

• Since the "as if" clause ("as if he has not slept") is already in the present perfect and describes his current look, the main verb must also be in the simple present: "He looks as if he has not slept."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "He has look" is grammatically wrong — the present perfect auxiliary "has" must be followed by a past participle ("looked"), not the base form "look".

• Option 3: "He was looking" incorrectly shifts the sentence into the Past Continuous Tense, but the sentence describes a present observation, not a past one.

• Option 4: "He will be look" is grammatically incorrect — the future continuous requires "will be + V-ing" (i.e. "will be looking"), not the bare form "look"; it also wrongly retains a future sense that is not needed for a present description.

NOTE

• "As if / as though" can also be followed by the Simple Past or Past Perfect to express something imaginary or contrary to fact (e.g. "He talks as if he knew everything" — implying he doesn't).

• Do not confuse this structural usage with real future or continuous action; when describing someone's present look/manner, use the simple present tense with "look/seem".

question:
Identify the correct spelling of the underlined word.
Medical termnalogy is difficult to understand.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. terminology.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "terminology" — meaning the body of specialized words or expressions used in a particular field, subject or profession.

• Spelling key: TERM + IN + OLOGY. The word begins with "term" (as in a specific expression), followed by "in", and ends with the suffix "-ology" (a common Greek-derived suffix meaning "the study of / a branch of knowledge").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tarmnalogy" is incorrect — the initial "term" has been wrongly spelt "tarm", and the middle syllables are jumbled.

• Option 2: "tarminology" is incorrect — the first syllable "ter" has been wrongly written as "tar".

• Option 4: "terminiology" is incorrect — an extra "i" has been wrongly inserted between "termin" and "ology".

NOTE

• Related words: term, terminal, terminate, terminology, terminological.

• Other frequently confused "-ology" spellings tested by SSC: technology, methodology, psychology, ideology, chronology — remember the consistent ending is "-ology", never "-alogy" or "-ollogy".

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person who loves and collects books
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Bibliophile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Bibliophile" is defined as a person who loves, collects and treasures books. (पुस्तक-प्रेमी)
◦ Example: As a true bibliophile, she owns thousands of rare first editions.

• Word origin: from the Greek "biblion" (book) + "philos" (loving) — the same root "philos" appears in many one-word substitutes ending in "-phile" that mean "a lover of ___".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Philanthropist" (परोपकारी व्यक्ति) means a person who seeks to promote the welfare of others, especially through the donation of money, not a lover of books.

• Option 3: "Geologist" (भूविज्ञानी) means a person who studies the physical structure and substance of the earth, its rocks and strata, entirely unrelated to books.

• Option 4: "Sommelier" (मद्य विशेषज्ञ) means a waiter or expert who specialises in wines, unrelated to books.

NOTE

• Other "-phile" one-word substitutes tested by SSC: Anglophile (a lover of England/English things), Cynophile (a lover of dogs), Xenophile (a lover of foreign things/people).

• Related book-themed one-word substitutes: Bibliomaniac (one who is excessively/obsessively fond of collecting books), Bibliopole (a person who deals in books, especially rare ones).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Amateur
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Professional.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Amateur" means a person who engages in an activity, sport or study as a pastime rather than as a profession, often lacking expert skill. (शौकिया/अव्यवसायी व्यक्ति)

• Its direct antonym is "Professional", meaning a person engaged in a specified activity as one's main paid occupation, possessing expert skill and training. (व्यवसायी/निपुण व्यक्ति)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Hobbyist" means a person who pursues a particular activity or interest in their spare time, for pleasure, which is actually very close to the meaning of "amateur" itself, not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Devotee" means a person who is very interested in and enthusiastic about someone or something, again close to an amateur enthusiast, not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Layman" means a person without professional or specialised knowledge in a particular subject, which is a near-synonym of "amateur" (both denote a non-expert), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Related word pairs frequently tested by SSC: Novice x Expert, Beginner x Veteran, Dilettante x Specialist — all following the same "non-expert vs expert" pattern as Amateur x Professional.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom for the underlined words in the given sentence.
The candidate blamed the persistent traffic jam as reason of his being late and the interviewer believed him though he was not convinced.
option_3: thought err is human and to forgive is divine
option_4: did not judge the book by its cover
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. gave the benefit of doubt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to give (someone) the benefit of the doubt" means to believe or accept someone's explanation without being fully certain or convinced that it is true, choosing to trust them despite lingering doubt. (शक होते हुए भी भरोसा कर लेना)
◦ Example: Although her excuse sounded unlikely, the teacher gave her the benefit of the doubt.

• This matches the underlined portion exactly: the interviewer believed the candidate even though he was not fully convinced by the traffic-jam excuse — precisely what "giving the benefit of the doubt" means.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "changed his tune" (रुख बदलना): means to alter one's opinion or attitude, often suddenly — there is no indication in the sentence that the interviewer changed any earlier stance.

• Option 3: "thought err is human and to forgive is divine" (गलती करना मानवीय है, क्षमा करना ईश्वरीय): conveys forgiving a fault/mistake, but here the interviewer is not forgiving a wrongdoing — he is choosing to believe an explanation despite doubt, a different idea.

• Option 4: "did not judge the book by its cover" (बाहरी रूप से किसी का मूल्यांकन न करना): means not to form an opinion about someone/something based only on outward appearance — irrelevant here, as the passage is about accepting an excuse, not about appearances.

NOTE

• Other trust/doubt-related idioms tested by SSC: "To take at face value" (to accept something as it appears, without questioning), "To have a leap of faith" (to trust something without proof), "To smell a rat" (to suspect something is wrong).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
Caves like Ajanta lie in perpetual darkness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Permanent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Perpetual" means never ending or changing; continuing forever or for a very long time. (चिरस्थायी/सतत)
◦ Example: The old lighthouse stood in perpetual silence, far from any town.

• "Permanent" means lasting or intended to last indefinitely; not temporary, which conveys the same sense of unending continuity as "perpetual", making it the closest synonym among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Extreme" means very great in degree; far from moderate, describing intensity, not permanence — it does not capture the "never-ending" sense of "perpetual".

• Option 3: "Brief" means lasting only a short time, which is actually opposite in meaning to "perpetual".

• Option 4: "Huge" means extremely large in size or amount, describing magnitude, not duration — unrelated to the intended sense.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Perpetual": eternal, everlasting, incessant, ceaseless, unending, constant.

• Do not confuse "perpetual" (continuing forever) with "perennial" (recurring again and again, or lasting through the year), which is a commonly confused pair in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Comply
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Deny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Comply" means to act in accordance with a wish, request, rule or command; to agree to do what is asked. (अनुपालन करना/मान लेना)

• "Deny" means to refuse to agree to or comply with (a request or demand); to state that something is not true or to refuse to give something, which is the direct opposite of willingly agreeing/obeying, making it the best antonym here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Engage" means to participate or become involved in an activity, which is unrelated to obedience or refusal — not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Assist" means to help someone, typically by doing a share of the work, which is unrelated to compliance or refusal.

• Option 4: "Expect" means to regard something as likely to happen, a word about anticipation, not about obeying or refusing — unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Comply": obey, conform, adhere, abide by, submit to.

• Other antonym pairs on the same theme frequently tested by SSC: Obey x Defy, Conform x Rebel, Submit x Resist.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options.
The sun / revolves / around / a earth.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. a earth.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Use of Articles: The indefinite article "a" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound, while "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound. Additionally, unique nouns like "the earth", "the sun", "the moon", "the sky" conventionally take the definite article "the", not an indefinite article, since there is only one earth.

• The error lies in the phrase "a earth" — it should be corrected to "the earth", giving the grammatically correct sentence: "The sun revolves around the earth."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "The sun" is correct — "the" is rightly used before the unique noun "sun".

• Option 2: "revolves" is correct — the verb correctly takes the third-person singular "-s" form to agree with the singular subject "The sun".

• Option 4: "around" is correct — it is the appropriate preposition to describe a circular/orbital motion.

NOTE

• Unique natural objects such as the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky, the world, the universe always take the definite article "the", never "a/an".

• "A" is used before a consonant sound (a university, a European) and "an" before a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA) — the rule depends on pronunciation, not the written first letter.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
(A) between the two countries
(B) will inevitably count
(C) the recent political incident
(D) against the peace process
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. CABD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must begin with a clear subject. Part (C) "the recent political incident" is the natural subject of the sentence, so it must come first.

• The subject needs to be described further before the verb: (A) "between the two countries" logically follows (C), specifying which incident is being spoken of, giving "the recent political incident between the two countries".

• This complete subject is then followed by the verb phrase (B) "will inevitably count", and finally by (D) "against the peace process", which completes the meaning of the verb "count against".

• Arranging as C-A-B-D gives: "The recent political incident between the two countries will inevitably count against the peace process." — a complete and meaningful sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "CDBA" produces "the recent political incident against the peace process will inevitably count between the two countries", which is grammatically incoherent and changes the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "CDAB" produces "the recent political incident against the peace process between the two countries will inevitably count", an awkward and meaningless string of prepositional phrases with no proper verb placement.

• Option 3: "CBAD" produces "the recent political incident will inevitably count between the two countries against the peace process", which misplaces "between the two countries" and disrupts the logical flow.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-jumbling questions, first identify the subject phrase, then the verb phrase, and finally the modifying/prepositional phrases — arranging Subject + Verb + Modifiers in the most natural English word order usually gives the correct sequence.

• The phrasal verb "count against" means "to be a factor working to someone's/something's disadvantage" — recognising fixed phrasal verbs helps identify which parts must stay adjacent.

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
A. or brave man to make
B. money the chief object of his thoughts
C. for a well-educated, intellectual
D. it is physically impossible
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. DCAB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence must open with a subject-verb structure introducing the idea. Part (D) "it is physically impossible" is the only part that can grammatically begin the sentence, since it contains the subject "it" and the main verb "is".

• "Impossible" needs to be followed by "for + person", so (C) "for a well-educated, intellectual" logically follows (D), beginning the description of the person being spoken about.

• This description of the person is completed by (A) "or brave man to make", which finishes the list "well-educated, intellectual or brave man" and introduces the infinitive "to make".

• Finally, (B) "money the chief object of his thoughts" completes the infinitive phrase "to make money the chief object of his thoughts".

• Arranging as D-C-A-B gives: "It is physically impossible for a well-educated, intellectual or brave man to make money the chief object of his thoughts." — a complete, meaningful sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "ABCD" begins with "or brave man to make", which cannot start a sentence since it opens with the conjunction "or" and lacks a subject.

• Option 3: "CDAB" begins with "for a well-educated, intellectual", which also cannot start a sentence as "for" here functions as a preposition requiring a preceding clause ("it is impossible for...").

• Option 4: "CABD" similarly begins with the prepositional phrase "for a well-educated, intellectual", which cannot stand as the opening of a grammatically complete sentence.

NOTE

• In such jumbling questions, look for the part containing the finite verb and subject ("it is...") — that part must open the sentence, since prepositional or conjunction-led fragments cannot stand alone as sentence openers.

• Watch for infinitive-phrase splits (e.g. "to make ... the chief object") — the two halves of a single infinitive phrase must always be placed together.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Mahesh's attitude annoyed me and I blew into.
option_1: annoyed me and I blew over
option_2: annoyed me and I blew off
option_3: annoyed me and I blew down of
option_4: annoyed me and I blew up
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. annoyed me and I blew up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "to blow up" means to suddenly become very angry; to lose one's temper. (अचानक बहुत गुस्सा हो जाना)
◦ Example: My father blew up when he saw the dented car.

• The original sentence "Mahesh's attitude annoyed me and I blew into" is grammatically incomplete — "blew into" is not a recognised idiomatic phrase in this context. Since the first clause already establishes anger ("annoyed me"), the second clause logically continues with "I blew up", meaning the speaker's annoyance turned into an outburst of anger.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "blew over" means (of a storm, trouble or scandal) to pass or come to an end without serious consequence — this describes a situation calming down, the opposite of losing one's temper.

• Option 2: "blew off" typically means to skip or fail to attend something (e.g. "blew off the meeting"), or informally "to release pent-up energy" — it does not fit the sense of suddenly getting angry as well as "blew up" does, and is not the phrase completed grammatically here.

• Option 3: "blew down of" is not a standard English phrasal verb; "blow down" (without "of") means to be knocked down by wind, which is unrelated to anger and grammatically wrong with the added "of".

NOTE

• Other anger-related phrasal verbs/idioms tested by SSC: "to fly off the handle" (to lose one's temper suddenly), "to hit the roof" (to become extremely angry), "to see red" (to become very angry).

• Do not confuse "blow up" (lose temper / explode) with "blow over" (a problem subsiding) and "blow off" (to skip/dismiss something) — all three use "blow" but carry very different meanings.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the word 'Pervasive' from the given sentence.
The scientist's hypothesis was substantiated by extensive research and experimentation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Extensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Pervasive" means spreading widely throughout an area or a group of people; existing in or affecting every part of something. (सर्वव्यापी/व्यापक)

• Among the words present in the given sentence, "Extensive", meaning covering or affecting a large area; wide-ranging in scope, is the closest in meaning to "pervasive", since both words describe something that is widespread or covers a broad scope.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Substantiated" means provided with evidence to support or prove the truth of something, which relates to proof/confirmation, not to the idea of being "widespread".

• Option 3: "Experimentation" means the action of trying out new ideas or methods, especially in science, referring to a process or method, not to something being widespread.

• Option 4: "Hypothesis" means a supposition or proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence, referring to a tentative idea, unrelated to the sense of "pervasive".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Pervasive": widespread, prevalent, ubiquitous, universal, rife.

• Antonym of "Pervasive": rare, localized, limited, scarce — useful to recall since SSC sometimes frames the same word as an antonym-based question instead.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
The dog took a ________ during his walk and lifted his ________ to indicate that he was tired.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. pause; paws.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pause" means a temporary stop or break in action, which correctly fits the first blank — "The dog took a pause during his walk" (i.e. the dog stopped briefly).

• "Paws" refers to the feet of an animal that has claws or nails, which correctly fits the second blank — "lifted his paws" refers to the dog physically lifting its feet, a natural sign of tiredness.

• Both words together give the sensible sentence: "The dog took a pause during his walk and lifted his paws to indicate that he was tired."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "pause; pours" is incorrect for the second blank — "pours" (the verb form of "pour", meaning to flow or dispense liquid) makes no sense with "lifted his pours".

• Option 2: "pours; pores" is incorrect for both blanks — "pours" does not fit "took a pours", and "pores" (tiny openings in the skin) cannot be "lifted".

• Option 3: "paws; pause" reverses the correct pair — "took a paws" and "lifted his pause" are both nonsensical; the words must be used in the order pause-then-paws, not paws-then-pause.

NOTE

• Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning — always determine the correct word from the surrounding context/meaning of the sentence, not from sound alone.

• Other commonly tested homophone sets: there/their/they're, its/it's, whose/who's, principal/principle, stationary/stationery, weather/whether.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I have few deliberations for you. Don't leave your hard work to ____1____. If you have gone to the effort to complete a dialogue, ____2____ fritter away all the meaning you created by trusting your memories. Write down the ____3____ of conclusions, decisions and assignments. Remember to record ____4____ does what by when. Revisit your notes at key times and ____5____ assignments.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. memory.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Don't leave your hard work to ____1____." The passage as a whole warns against relying on one's memory** instead of writing things down — this is reinforced later by "trusting your memories" and "Write down the details...".

• "Memory" fits logically and grammatically: "Don't leave your hard work to memory" means "don't depend solely on remembering it", which sets up the passage's central advice to record things in writing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "diary" does not fit — one does not "leave work to a diary"; a diary is something you write in, not something you leave your work "to" in this idiomatic sense.

• Option 2: "notes" is grammatically awkward here and also contradicts the passage's later advice to actually "write down" details — the blank refers to what one should NOT depend on, which is memory, not notes.

• Option 4: "someone" does not fit the context — the passage is about personal record-keeping and self-reliance on memory versus writing, not about delegating work to another person.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always read the entire passage first before choosing an answer for any individual blank — later sentences (here, "trusting your memories") often confirm or hint at the correct word for an earlier blank.

• This is a classic "note-taking/productivity advice" passage type — expect vocabulary around remembering, recording, and reviewing.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I have few deliberations for you. Don't leave your hard work to ____1____. If you have gone to the effort to complete a dialogue, ____2____ fritter away all the meaning you created by trusting your memories. Write down the ____3____ of conclusions, decisions and assignments. Remember to record ____4____ does what by when. Revisit your notes at key times and ____5____ assignments.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. do not.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"If you have gone to the effort to complete a dialogue, ____2____ fritter away all the meaning you created by trusting your memories." The clause is an imperative/advisory instruction** (an instruction to the reader, addressed as "you"), continuing the tone of the earlier imperative "Don't leave your hard work to memory."

• Rule: A negative imperative/present-tense instruction addressed to "you" takes the auxiliary "do not" (don't), not "does not" (used for he/she/it) or "did not"/"had not" (used for past events).

• "do not fritter away" correctly continues the advisory, present-tense tone of the passage: "...do not fritter away all the meaning you created..."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "does not" is incorrect — "does not" is used with third-person singular subjects (he/she/it), but the passage is addressed directly to "you" (the reader), which takes "do not".

• Option 2: "did not" is incorrect — this would shift the sentence into the past tense, but the surrounding sentences ("Write down...", "Remember to record...", "Revisit your notes...") are all in the present/imperative, not the past.

• Option 4: "had not" is incorrect — "had not" is used with a past participle to form the past perfect negative (e.g. "had not fritted"), which does not fit grammatically before the base verb "fritter".

NOTE

• Imperative sentences (instructions/advice) are formed in the present tense and take "do not / don't" for their negative form, regardless of whether the subject "you" is stated or implied.

• Maintaining tense consistency across a passage is key in cloze questions — check the tense of the surrounding sentences before choosing an auxiliary verb.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 3.
solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Write down the ____3____ of conclusions, decisions and assignments."** The passage advises the reader to record specific, particular information about conclusions, decisions and assignments so that nothing is forgotten.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "titles" does not fit — one does not typically speak of the "titles" of conclusions, decisions and assignments; "titles" refers to names/headings, not the substantive content being recorded.

• Option 2: "failures" is contextually wrong — the passage is a positive, constructive piece of advice about recording useful information, not about writing down "failures".

• Option 4: "short cuts" does not fit logically — the passage is about being thorough and detailed in recording information, which is the opposite of taking "short cuts".

NOTE

• Cloze passages often test the ability to pick the word that best matches the overall tone and purpose of the passage — here, a tone of careful, thorough documentation, which rules out negative words like "failures" or contrary ideas like "short cuts".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I have few deliberations for you. Don't leave your hard work to ____1____. If you have gone to the effort to complete a dialogue, ____2____ fritter away all the meaning you created by trusting your memories. Write down the ____3____ of conclusions, decisions and assignments. Remember to record ____4____ does what by when. Revisit your notes at key times and ____5____ assignments.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. who.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Remember to record ____4____ does what by when." This is an embedded question asking about a person** — the sentence is essentially recording the answer to "Who does what by when?" (i.e., which person is responsible for which task, and by what deadline).

• Rule: The relative/interrogative pronoun "who" is used as the subject of a clause when referring to a person. Here, "____4____" is the subject of the verb "does", and it refers to a person (whoever is responsible), so "who" is correct: "...record who does what by when."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "which" is incorrect — "which" is used for things/animals, not for persons, and cannot be the subject referring to "the person who does something".

• Option 3: "that" is grammatically possible for a relative clause referring to a person in some contexts, but in this fixed idiomatic expression "who does what by when" (a well-known phrase for task-assignment tracking), the standard and most appropriate word is "who", making it a better fit than "that" here.

• Option 4: "whom" is incorrect — "whom" is the object form of "who", used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition; here, the pronoun is the subject of "does", so the subject form "who" is required, not "whom".

NOTE

• Who vs Whom: "Who" is used as a subject (Who did this?), while "Whom" is used as an object (To whom did you give it?/Whom did you meet?).

• "Which" is reserved for non-human things and animals without personal names, while "who/whom/that" can refer to people ("that" is more common in restrictive/defining clauses in informal usage).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

I have few deliberations for you. Don't leave your hard work to ____1____. If you have gone to the effort to complete a dialogue, ____2____ fritter away all the meaning you created by trusting your memories. Write down the ____3____ of conclusions, decisions and assignments. Remember to record ____4____ does what by when. Revisit your notes at key times and ____5____ assignments.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. review.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"Revisit your notes at key times and ____5____ assignments."** The verb must logically pair with "revisit your notes", continuing the idea of looking back over recorded information at important moments.

• "Review", meaning to examine or assess something again, especially in order to check it or make changes, fits perfectly alongside "revisit" — one revisits notes and reviews assignments, both being acts of checking recorded work.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "obliterate" means to destroy utterly; wipe out completely, which is the opposite of the passage's advice to preserve and check one's records.

• Option 2: "introspect" means to examine one's own thoughts or feelings, which applies to self-reflection on one's inner state, not to checking external assignments/tasks.

• Option 3: "speculate" means to form a theory without firm evidence; to guess, which does not fit the context of methodically checking recorded assignments.

NOTE

• The word "review" pairs naturally with "revisit" here — both imply returning to something already recorded to verify or reassess it, matching the overall theme of the passage (good note-taking and follow-up practice).

• Commonly confused words: "revise" (to re-examine and improve, especially written work) vs "review" (to examine again/assess) vs "revert" (to return to a previous state or topic).
